m-jacksonville|2025-02-04|d4f1cd71|ab32e.title: Steve Lundy, Deputy Director of the PFPF, made a presentation on the fund’s actuarial valuation report. He outlined the funding policy and said the City’s employer contribution next fiscal year is calculated at $201.4M, which is considerably higher than this year’s contribution due primarily to the raises the police and fire unions got this year and next in the recently approved contracts. The City’s contribution is considerably reduced by the future value of the pension sales tax. The actual surtax growth rate for last year was 2.4%, less than the target of 4.25%. The fund achieved a 20.4% return on investments last year, well above the target of 6.25%. The funded ratio of the plan is 44.1%, down from 44.7% last year. Council Member Lahnen asked about next year’s contribution increase. PFPF Executive Director Tim Johnson said it will be $23M more than previously projected by last year’s report which occurred before the collective bargaining raises were awarded. Council Member Howland asked about the timing for reaching full funding status; Mr. Lundy said estimated in 2056, which is 1 year later than previously projected but still far short of the 30- year life of the sales surtax. Mr. Johnson said the increase in the liability amount due to the negotiated raises was the cause of the 1-year extension to reach full funding, and that will change from year to year as participant demographics and investment returns change. This $23M change is a one-time item, $2-3M per year will

m-jacksonville|2025-02-13|ed621b5d|b62c3.title: Commissioner Hardesty began by expressing interest in hearing from the Northeast Florida Regional Council regarding its priorities, anticipating a robust discussion at a future meeting. He then focused his remarks on the topic of artificial reefs, noting that Jacksonville was once considered a national leader in reef development but has effectively been at a standstill since approximately 2009, when the city collaborated on the sinking a vessel known as “The Spike.” He explained that most subsequent reef initiatives in the area have come from the private sector, which has pushed them further. He stated that he had scheduled a meeting with Melissa Long, Chief of the Environmental Quality Division, on February 25th to discuss grant writing and funding opportunities for artificial reef projects. He also mentioned speaking with Mr. Keith Mille of the Florida Artificial Reef Program, who confirmed that Jacksonville has largely been inactive in this field for some time, partly due to turnover and the loss of key personnel who once managed grant applications and project coordination. He highlighted the significant economic and environmental benefits of artificial reefs, referencing data indicating a “$3.1 billion infusion” to the state’s economy from industries that utilize these structures, specifically recreational and commercial fishing. He pointed to Okaloosa County as an example, describing its “vibrant and active” artificial reef commission and the success it has achieved. Com
